title: Hanuman's pearls
hookLine: Sita's pearls go to Hanuman, the devotee who wants only Rama
carry: bhakti keeps god in the heart
last: DIWALI'S LAMPS WELCOME THE LIGHT HOME.

cards: A coronation is a strange kind of party. Everyone dresses up, there are speeches and gifts, and underneath it the whole room asks one question: what will this person do with the power?

Valmiki's crowning of Rama has all the glitter: water from the rivers and the seas, priests chanting, a brother holding the royal umbrella, allies waving the fans. But one moment people treasure is small.
It happens after the ceremony, between Sita and Hanuman, over a necklace.

teach.b: First, Rama cuts off the matted hair of the forest years and bathes. Then sacred water is poured over him: the abhisheka, the anointing that makes a king, led by the family priest Vasishtha.
Gifts go out to everyone, the monkey and bear allies too.
Rama gives Sita a necklace of pearls, and Sita keeps looking from the necklace to Hanuman. Rama sees it. Give it to the one you're most pleased with, he says.
She places it around Hanuman's neck: the one who found her in the ashoka grove when no one else could. Valmiki's scene ends there. But Hindus kept telling it.
In a much-loved later telling, not in Valmiki, Hanuman bites the pearls open one by one and drops them. The court is shocked.
I'm looking for Rama in them, he says, and he isn't there, so what are they worth? Someone mocks him: is Rama in you, then?

teach.h: BHAKTI KEEPS GOD IN THE HEART.
teach.b: Hanuman tears open his chest, and there in his heart sit Rama and Sita. You'll find that picture in many Hindu homes. It's bhakti, loving devotion, at its clearest: the devotee wants God, not God's gifts.

It's a big reason Hindus pray to Hanuman, the mightiest of Rama's allies, as the model devotee. Then Valmiki closes the war book. Rama rules a long, peaceful age; the rains come on time, and no child dies before a parent.
People still call a just order Rama Rajya. Some recitations stop right here. But the Ramayana as it has come down has one more book, and tomorrow it opens.

how: Many Hindu homes keep a picture of Hanuman with Rama and Sita in his opened chest, and many Hindus recite the Hanuman Chalisa, often on Tuesdays and Saturdays; many traditional Ramayana recitations end with Rama's coronation, the pattabhishekam.

o: the day Rama is first promised the throne
the festival of lamps that remembers Rama's return
the anointing bath that makes a prince into a king

p: the anointing that makes a king
a picture of a just reign

s: Sita gives her pearl necklace to Hanuman
Rama tells her to give it to the one she's most pleased with, and she chooses Hanuman.
Valmiki tells of Hanuman opening his chest to show Rama and Sita
that's a much-loved later telling; in Valmiki, Sita simply gives him the pearls.
in the later telling, Hanuman breaks the pearls because he's searching for Rama in them
if Rama isn't in them, he asks, what are they worth?

games.q: you're Hanuman, wearing a queen's pearls in a hall full of heroes. in the later telling, what do you do with them?
o: wear them proudly; you earned them.
search them for Rama, and set them aside when he isn't there.
give them to Sugriva, your king.
games.why: the devotee wants God, not the gifts. that's bhakti, and one big reason Hindus pray to Hanuman as the model devotee.

practice: Sit and rest a hand over your heart. Many Hindus repeat a name of God through the day. Try Sita Ram, softly, on each breath out, for a minute or two, as if you're keeping them there, the way Hanuman does in the picture.
If you don't pray, hold someone you love in that place instead, and breathe their name.

wordCard.voice: Diwali. The festival of lamps that, for many Hindus, remembers Rama coming home; and the homecoming ends here, in a crowning, a necklace on Hanuman, and the just reign the tradition calls Rama Rajya.

orig.note: Sanskrit bhakti: devotion, from bhaj, to share in, to love and serve.

carryVoice: Your line: bhakti keeps god in the heart. Hanuman wanted Rama, not pearls. Day six hundred sixty-three counts.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda 128 (the coronation; the necklace; Rama's reign; the closing blessing)
